claims.text: Differences in deformation behavior among equiatomic Cr-Mn-Fe-Co-Ni and its quaternary and ternary subsets arise from differences in local chemical short-range order.
Differences in failure behavior among these alloys arise from differences in local chemical short-range order.
Concomitant lattice distortion contributes to the differences in deformation and failure behavior.
Local chemical ordering and lattice distortion alter dislocation mobility.
Local chemical ordering and lattice distortion alter operative deformation mechanisms.
Substitutional disorder produces local chemical short-range order and lattice distortion in these alloys.
Different combinations of Cr, Mn, Fe, Co, and Ni produce different local atomic arrangements.
Lower-constituent-count alloys can have greater short-range order than the equiatomic quinary alloy.
Greater short-range order can increase dislocation pinning.
Greater short-range order can alter the active slip systems.
The equiatomic quinary alloy has a more homogeneous chemical environment than its lower-component subsets.
The quinary alloy's more homogeneous chemical environment may permit easier dislocation motion or different twinning behavior.
Relative to equiatomic Cr-Mn-Fe-Co-Ni, alloys with fewer constituents will exhibit increased short-range order or local clustering.
Increased local order will correlate with changes in measured mechanical response.
Lower-component alloys with increased local order are expected to have higher yield strength than the equiatomic quinary baseline.
Lower-component alloys with increased local order are expected to have a modified work-hardening rate relative to the equiatomic quinary baseline.
Increased resistance to dislocation motion explains the predicted strengthening associated with increased local order.
The proposed relationship is limited to thermomechanically processed, single-phase FCC alloys and may not apply when phase separation, intermetallics, or dominant grain-boundary effects are present.
